What's new in emergency medicine

Authors:[Michael Ganetsky, MD](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/contributors)[Jonathan S Grayzel, MD](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/contributors)[James F Wiley, II, MD, MPH](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/contributors)

Please read the [Disclaimer](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/8365/print#disclaimerContent)at the end of this page.

The following represent additions to UpToDate from the past six months that were considered by the editors and authors to be of particular interest. The most recent What's New entries are at the top of each subsection.

ADULT RESUSCITATION

Catheter-directed thrombolysis versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), limited data suggest that catheter-directed thrombolysis improves RV function compared with anticoagulation alone, but does not improve mortality. In a recent randomized trial of 544 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE, ultrasound-facilitated, catheter-directed thrombolysis with [alteplase](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/alteplase-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) reduced the composite outcome of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation, or symptomatic PE recurrence compared with anticoagulation alone (4 versus 10 percent); this difference was driven primarily by fewer episodes of decompensation (3.7 versus 10.3 percent) [[1](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/1)]. Major bleeding was numerically higher in the alteplase group (4 versus 2 percent) but was not statistically significant, and the difference in RV size at 48 hours between the two groups was also not significant. Interpretation is limited by low event rates, lack of blinding, and underrepresentation of patients >75 years. However, these data support our practice of performing catheter-directed therapies in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Catheter-directed thrombolysis'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Catheter-directed+thrombolysis&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4140125415&source=see_link#H4140125415).)

Updated international Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (March 2026)

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines have recently been updated [[2](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/2)]. The guidelines suggested that, while a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg should be targeted, a range of 60 to 70 mmHg is practical for most adults with sepsis. The guidelines also emphasized the importance of screening tools for early detection and management of sepsis, while discouraging both overly aggressive fluid resuscitation and empiric treatment for fungal and anaerobic bacterial infections, especially when suspicion is low. The guidelines encouraged active fluid removal (in the later phases of shock), rapid de-escalation of antimicrobials and, in mechanically ventilated patients, the use of selective digestive tract decontamination to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia. We agree with these recommendations. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Introduction'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=INTRODUCTION&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1&source=see_link#H1).)

Joint European and United States definition of refractory septic shock (March 2026)

Although sepsis and septic shock have widely accepted definitions, there has not been consensus regarding the definition of "refractory" septic shock. The Society of Critical Care Medicine and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine have recently proposed criteria defining refractory septic shock by the presence of (1) persistently elevated lactate concentration (>2 mmol/L [>18 mg/dL]) and/or prolonged capillary refill time, (2) lack of response to fluid resuscitation, (3) a norepinephrine base equivalent dose >0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute, and (4) in those with suspected mixed shock, critical care ultrasound should be used to confirm lack of response to fluids and to exclude other etiologies for shock [[3](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/3)]. The impact of this definition on patient outcomes, such as survival, remains undetermined. (See ["Sepsis syndromes in adults: Epidemiology, definitions, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and prognosis", section on 'Septic shock'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sepsis-syndromes-in-adults-epidemiology-definitions-clinical-presentation-diagnosis-and-prognosis?sectionName=Septic+shock&topicRef=8365&anchor=H8&source=see_link#H8).)

High-flow oxygen does not affect mortality in hypoxemic respiratory failure (March 2026)

Although frequently used, the value of high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure remains unclear. In a randomized trial of 1110 such patients, HFNC did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with low-flow oxygen [[4](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/4)]. HFNC led to a non-significant reduction in the intubation rate at 28 days (42.4 versus 48.4 percent), and rapidly improved patients' respiratory rates, dyspnea, and carbon dioxide levels. These data support our practice of administering HFNC only to patients with advanced oxygen needs (eg, >6 L/minute) rather than routine administration. (See ["Evaluation and management of the nonventilated, hospitalized adult patient with acute hypoxemia", section on 'Humidified, high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-the-nonventilated-hospitalized-adult-patient-with-acute-hypoxemia?sectionName=Humidified%2C+high-flow+oxygen+delivered+via+nasal+cannulae+%28HFNC%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3611214250&source=see_link#H3611214250).)

Updated resuscitation guidelines for adults (January 2026)

The American Heart Association and European Resuscitation Council have published updated guidelines for adult cardiopulmonary resuscitation and emergency care [[5,6](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/5,6)]. Resuscitation updates include: urgent electrical cardioversion for patients who are unstable and those with rate-related ischemia caused by atrial fibrillation or flutter; immediate defibrillation for all adult patients with sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; and increased support for using extracorporeal devices for potentially reversible causes of cardiac arrest where resources are available. Post-resuscitation updates include a normocapnic ventilation target and recommendations for a target temperature ≤37.5°C for a minimum of 36 hours following return of spontaneous circulation. (See ["Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) in adults", section on 'Management of specific arrhythmias'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/advanced-cardiac-life-support-acls-in-adults?sectionName=MANAGEMENT+OF+SPECIFIC+ARRHYTHMIAS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H7&source=see_link#H7) and ["Intensive care unit management of the intubated post-cardiac arrest adult patient", section on 'Setting the target temperature'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/intensive-care-unit-management-of-the-intubated-post-cardiac-arrest-adult-patient?sectionName=Setting+the+target+temperature&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1286775785&source=see_link#H1286775785).)

Induction and tracheal intubation in critically ill patients using etomidate or ketamine (December 2025)

Concern exists regarding induction with [etomidate](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/etomidate-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) during rapid sequence intubation (RSI) in critically ill patients, particularly septic patients, because of transient adrenocortical suppression that may worsen outcomes. [Ketamine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ketamine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) has been proposed as an alternative for such patients, but it stimulates catecholamine release and may increase risk of myocardial ischemia or pulmonary hypertension. A pragmatic trial of more than 2300 critically ill adults undergoing RSI in the emergency department or intensive care unit found similar in-hospital 28-day mortality between the ketamine and etomidate groups (28 versus 29 percent) [[7](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/7)]. Almost half of the patients had sepsis or septic shock, also with no difference in mortality (39 versus 38 percent). These findings suggest that either etomidate or ketamine is a reasonable induction agent in critically ill patients, including those with sepsis. (See ["General anesthesia: Intravenous induction agents", section on 'Disadvantages and adverse effects'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/general-anesthesia-intravenous-induction-agents?sectionName=Disadvantages+and+adverse+effects&topicRef=8365&anchor=H262499028&source=see_link#H262499028).)

Updated sequential organ failure assessment score (SOFA-2) (December 2025)

An updated Sepsis Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, termed SOFA-2, has been published [[8](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/8)]. SOFA-2 resolves many of the deficiencies of SOFA-1 (eg, inclusion of a broader range of organ failure thresholds in the original six organ domains). Data from over 2 million patients in over 1300 intensive care units (ICUs) were used to develop and validate the score in all-comer ICU patients. SOFA-2 and SOFA-1 demonstrated a similar ability to predict ICU mortality. A 1-point increase in SOFA-2 increased the odds of ICU mortality (odds ratio, 1.378). Sequential SOFA-2 calculations from ICU day 1 to 7 remained predictive throughout those seven days. We agree with the updated version of SOFA; however, it does not automatically change the SOFA-1-based Sepsis-3 definition for sepsis and septic shock. (See ["Predictive scoring systems in the intensive care unit", section on 'Sequential (sepsis-related) Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/predictive-scoring-systems-in-the-intensive-care-unit?sectionName=Sequential+%28sepsis-related%29+Organ+Failure+Assessment+%28SOFA%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H889841588&source=see_link#H889841588).)

Arterial catheter in shock (December 2025)

Whether an arterial catheter should be routinely inserted in patients with shock is unclear. A recent trial reported outcomes comparing arterial catheter placement with no catheter in over 1000 patients with shock, half of whom had sepsis [[9](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/9)]. Ninety-day mortality was similar between the two groups (34 versus 37 percent). Pain, hemorrhage, and hematoma were more common in the arterial catheter group. Limitations of the study include a lack of blinding, baseline group differences, and limited applicability to specific types of shock. Nonetheless, these results suggest that many patients can be managed without an arterial catheter, although our approach is to place an arterial catheter when a reasonable indication is present (eg, labile blood pressure, unreliable blood pressure readings). (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Monitoring catheters'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=Monitoring+catheters&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3514478798&source=see_link#H3514478798).)

Capillary refill time as a tissue perfusion biomarker in septic shock (December 2025)

Preliminary data suggest that using capillary refill time (CRT) as a clinical biomarker of tissue perfusion may lower mortality in patients with septic shock. In a recent trial, a protocol that used CRT to tailor fluid, vasopressor, and inotrope therapy was compared with usual care in over 1500 patients with early septic shock [[10](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/10)]. The CRT protocol reduced the duration of vital organ support by 5 percent. The CRT group also received less fluid and had a higher percentage of patients receiving vasopressor therapy. However, mortality was similar, the trial was unblinded, and the impact of the additional components of the CRT protocol on outcomes was not accurately assessed. Nonetheless, these data support our practice of including CRT as part of the bedside assessment when monitoring the response to therapy in patients with septic shock. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Clinical'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=Clinical&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1643153952&source=see_link#H1643153952).)

Tracheoarterial fistula: A large series description (December 2025)

Tracheoarterial fistula is a late, life-threatening complication of tracheostomy placement associated with high mortality. In a series date of almost 150 patients, the median time to fistula development was 80 days [[11](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/11)]. Only half of patients had the classic feature of an initial small "sentinel" bleed followed by massive hemorrhage a few hours or days later. Imaging (typically computed tomography) was better at diagnosing the fistula than bronchoscopy (80 versus 32 percent). Tracheostomy cuff overinflation and sternal notch pressure controlled the bleeding in over 70 percent of patients while waiting for definitive therapy (ie, endovascular or surgical repair). These data inform early recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of the most fatal complication of tracheostomy. (See ["Tracheostomy: Postoperative care, maintenance, and complications in adults", section on 'Tracheoarterial fistula'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/tracheostomy-postoperative-care-maintenance-and-complications-in-adults?sectionName=Tracheoarterial+fistula&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3292466807&source=see_link#H3292466807).)

ENVIRONMENTAL EMERGENCIES

Iloprost for amputation prevention in frostbite (May 2026)

[Iloprost](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/iloprost-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is a prostacyclin analog that is indicated for the treatment of grade 3 or 4 frostbite (ie, cyanosis that extends proximal to the distal phalanx after rewarming), but supporting evidence is limited. In a study with over 250 patients (80 receiving iloprost) in two Canadian regions that differed in routine iloprost use but with a standardized frostbite care pathway, iloprost was associated with a lower amputation rate for grade 3 frostbite (30 versus 53 percent) but not for grade 2 and 4 frostbite; patients receiving a higher total iloprost dose were less likely to have amputations [[12](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/12)]. In 40 patients with grade 4 frostbite, iloprost treatment was associated with fewer finger and toe segment amputations (40 versus 51 percent and 47 versus 58 percent, respectively). These findings support our recommendation for iloprost in patients with severe frostbite. (See ["Frostbite: Acute care and prevention", section on 'Iloprost within 72 hours'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/frostbite-acute-care-and-prevention?sectionName=Iloprost+within+72+hours&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1902794625&source=see_link#H1902794625).)

Microorganisms in children with freshwater drowning-associated pneumonia (February 2026)

Infection with gram-negative organisms, especially _Aeromonas_ species, is predominantly reported in patients with drowning-associated pneumonia (DAP). In a study from China of over 70 children with freshwater DAP in a pediatric intensive care unit, _Staphylococcus aureus_ was the most isolated organism [[13](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/13)]. Other common pathogens included _Mycoplasma pneumoniae_, _Streptococcus pneumoniae_, _Haemophilus influenzae_, _Klebsiella pneumoniae_, _Candida albicans_, and rhinovirus. These findings highlight the need for an empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen, including coverage of gram-positive bacteria, in children with suspected DAP. (See ["Drowning (submersion injuries)", section on 'Pneumonia'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/drowning-submersion-injuries?sectionName=Pneumonia&topicRef=8365&anchor=H809358478&source=see_link#H809358478).)

Effectiveness of defibrillation in patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable rhythm (February 2026)

Patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable arrhythmias are less likely to have return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with defibrillation at a core temperature <30°C (86°F). Current recommendations are to attempt defibrillation with up to three shocks but withhold further attempts pending rewarming since cold myocardium can potentially be injured. A registry-based study with almost 40 patients with cardiac arrest, a shockable rhythm, and core temperature <30°C found that ROSC was more likely if defibrillation was performed during rewarming, as compared with before rewarming (100 versus 25 percent) [[14](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/14)]. Defibrillation during extracorporeal life support (ECLS) had a fivefold increase in odds of ROSC. These findings support our recommendations to attempt defibrillation even with temperature <30°C and to not withhold defibrillation during ECLS rewarming at temperature >25°C (77°F). (See ["Accidental hypothermia in adults: Management", section on 'Ventricular arrhythmias or asystole'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/accidental-hypothermia-in-adults-management?sectionName=Ventricular+arrhythmias+or+asystole&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1808505299&source=see_link#H1808505299).)

Acute hypersensitivity reactions from rattlesnake antivenom in alpha-gal endemic region (February 2026)

CroFab and Anavip, antivenoms used to treat Crotalinae snakebite envenomation, can potentially cause severe allergic reactions. Anavip contains more of the carbohydrate moiety galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (which is responsible for alpha-gal syndrome) compared with CroFab. A study with over 200 patients in Arkansas (a state with a high rate of alpha-gal sensitization) who received either Anavip or CroFab found that Anavip was associated with increased adverse drug reactions (including presumed anaphylaxis) compared with CroFab (22 versus 4 percent) [[15](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/15)]. Basophil activation testing from individuals with known alpha-gal syndrome found that Anavip more potently activated alpha-gal sensitized basophils. Clinicians who treat snakebite victims in regions with high rates of alpha-gal sensitization must be ready to manage anaphylaxis following antivenom (especially Anavip) administration. (See ["Bites by Crotalinae snakes (rattlesnakes, cottonmouths [water moccasins], or copperheads) in the United States: Management", section on 'Acute antivenom hypersensitivity reactions'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/bites-by-crotalinae-snakes-rattlesnakes-cottonmouths-water-moccasins-or-copperheads-in-the-united-states-management?sectionName=Acute+antivenom+hypersensitivity+reactions&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4098260420&source=see_link#H4098260420).)

GENERAL ADULT EMERGENCY MEDICINE

Fosphenytoin for trigeminal neuralgia attacks (May 2026)

Several pharmacologic options are available to treat acute trigeminal neuralgia (TN) pain, but available supporting evidence is limited. In a randomized trial that included 22 patients with acute TN symptoms, pain reduction on the numerical rating scale (0 for no pain up to 10 for worst pain) was greater at two hours among those assigned to [fosphenytoin](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fosphenytoin-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) than placebo (-6.1 versus -2.4) [[16](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/16)]. Treatment consisted of a loading dose followed by once daily maintenance treatment for up to four days. Patients assigned to fosphenytoin also had a higher rate of >50 percent pain reduction and reduction in the frequency of attack recurrence, and treatment was generally well tolerated. These data provide clinical trial evidence to support the role of fosphenytoin for acute TN exacerbations. (See ["Trigeminal neuralgia", section on 'Acute rescue therapy for patients with breakthrough pain'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/trigeminal-neuralgia?sectionName=Acute+rescue+therapy+for+patients+with+breakthrough+pain&topicRef=8365&anchor=H372586115&source=see_link#H372586115).)

AHA/ACC guidelines for pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

Several societies, including the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC), have issued joint guidelines for the evaluation and management of pulmonary embolism (PE) [[17](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/17)]. The guidelines stratify patients by risk of PE-related death to facilitate management. Patients in category A (incidental PE), B (symptomatic PE with a low clinical severity score), and C (symptomatic PE with an elevated clinical severity score) require anticoagulation. Patients in category D (incipient cardiopulmonary failure) and E (cardiopulmonary failure) are candidates for reperfusion therapies (eg, thrombectomy or thrombolysis, if they have a low bleeding risk). We await adoption of this classification and encourage its use to facilitate management. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Treatment overview and prognosis", section on 'American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/others'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-treatment-overview-and-prognosis?sectionName=American+Heart+Association%2FAmerican+College+of+Cardiology%2Fothers&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2148862999&source=see_link#H2148862999).)

Age-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs in deep vein thrombosis diagnosis (January 2026)

D-dimer values rise with age, decreasing specificity in older patients when a fixed cutoff is used to diagnose deep venous thrombosis (DVT). In a study of 2169 patients with low to moderate pretest probability for DVT, using an age-adjusted D-dimer (age [years] x 10 ng/mL for patients >50 years) compared with a fixed conventional cutoff of 500 ng/mL resulted in a 7 percent absolute increase in patients for whom DVT was excluded without lower extremity compression ultrasonography [[18](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/18)]. At three months, there were no VTE events in patients with a D-dimer level ≥500 ng/mL but below the age-adjusted cutoff. These data strengthen the case for more widespread utilization of age-adjusted D-dimer to diagnose DVT in older adults. (See ["Clinical presentation and diagnosis of the nonpregnant adult with suspected deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremity", section on 'Adjusted cutoffs'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/clinical-presentation-and-diagnosis-of-the-nonpregnant-adult-with-suspected-deep-vein-thrombosis-of-the-lower-extremity?sectionName=Adjusted+cutoffs&topicRef=8365&anchor=H410968138&source=see_link#H410968138).)

Andexanet alfa removed from the United States market (January 2026)

[Andexanet alfa](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/andexanet-alfa-inactivated-coagulation-factor-xa-recombinant-united-states-withdrawn-from-market-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), a specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors that was approved in 2018, has been removed from the United States market, as reported in a communication from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) [[19](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/19)]. The communication mentions concerns about an increased rate of serious thrombotic complications compared with usual care in the ANNEXA-I trial and states that the company has voluntarily withdrawn the licensing application for commercial reasons. For life-threatening bleeding associated with factor Xa inhibitors, 4-factor unactivated prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) can be used along with other hemostatic measures. (See ["Management of bleeding in patients receiving direct oral anticoagulants", section on 'Andexanet alfa'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/management-of-bleeding-in-patients-receiving-direct-oral-anticoagulants?sectionName=Andexanet+alfa&topicRef=8365&anchor=H635532401&source=see_link#H635532401) and ["Hemostatic treatments for anticoagulated patients with intracranial hemorrhage", section on 'Andexanet alfa if PCC is unavailable'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/hemostatic-treatments-for-anticoagulated-patients-with-intracranial-hemorrhage?sectionName=Andexanet+alfa+if+PCC+is+unavailable&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4272016095&source=see_link#H4272016095).)

Suction embolectomy versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (January 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), catheter-directed embolectomy is commonly performed but has not been compared with anticoagulation alone. In a recent randomized trial of 100 such patients, suction embolectomy followed by anticoagulation did not improve mortality but did result in a greater reduction of the right ventricular (RV)/left ventricular (LV) ratio (an indicator of RV strain) compared with anticoagulation alone (0.52 versus 0.24) [[20](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/20)]. In addition, normalization of tachycardia and indicators of pulmonary artery obstruction improved in a larger proportion of patients undergoing embolectomy. The adverse event rate (including bleeding) was similar between the groups, as was the need for intensive care unit admission and hospital length of stay; PE did not recur in either group. This study provides additional support for the use of catheter-directed embolectomy in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE with the goal of faster thrombus resolution and reduction in RV load. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Suction/mechanical embolectomy'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Suction%2Fmechanical+embolectomy&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3973928105&source=see_link#H3973928105).)

Post-thoracentesis ultrasonography for residual fluid evaluation (December 2025)

With the routine use of lung ultrasonography for therapeutic thoracentesis, it is unclear whether post-procedure chest radiography to still necessary to assess for residual fluid. In a recent prospective study of 147 patients with a free-flowing pleural effusion, there was excellent agreement between lung ultrasonography (performed immediately after the procedure) and chest radiography (performed four hours after thoracentesis; Gwet's agreement coefficient 0.93) [[21](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/21)]. There was also strong agreement between the proceduralist's interpretation and that of the blind ultrasound reviewer (kappa 0.81). These results suggest that ultrasonography is sufficient for evaluating residual fluid after thoracentesis; however, these findings may not be generalizable to patients with trapped lung and need additional study. (See ["Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis", section on 'Follow-up'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ultrasound-guided-thoracentesis?sectionName=FOLLOW-UP&topicRef=8365&anchor=H9&source=see_link#H9).)

GENERAL PEDIATRIC EMERGENCY MEDICINE

Pediatric sepsis hospitalization and mortality in the United States (March 2026)

New estimates of United States sepsis hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality based on a pediatric sepsis event definition derived from the 2024 Phoenix sepsis criteria have been reported using electronic-health record surveillance of clinical data from over 3.9 million pediatric hospitalizations (neonates excluded) from 2016 to 2023. The average annual hospital incidence of sepsis was 1.3 percent (over 18,000 annual cases); overall in-hospital mortality was 10.1 percent (over 1800 annual deaths) [[22,23](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/22,23)]. Annualized national estimates remained stable over the study period. These findings update prior sepsis estimates based upon older definitions of pediatric sepsis and confirm the high burden of pediatric illness due to sepsis in the United States. (See ["Sepsis in children: Definitions, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis", section on 'Burden of disease'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sepsis-in-children-definitions-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Burden+of+disease&topicRef=8365&anchor=H632992306&source=see_link#H632992306).)

Ibuprofen for acute pediatric musculoskeletal injuries (January 2026)

Most experts recommend nonopioid medications as first-line therapy for acute pain in children. However, for children with acute musculoskeletal injuries (eg, fractures and sprains), some clinicians and caregivers have concerns that pain could be undertreated without opioids. A recent trial randomly assigned nearly 700 children with nonoperative musculoskeletal extremity injuries (primarily nondisplaced fractures and sprains) and moderate pain to [ibuprofen](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ibuprofen-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) alone, ibuprofen plus [acetaminophen](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acetaminophen-paracetamol-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), or ibuprofen plus an oral opioid ([hydromorphone](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/hydromorphone-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) [[24](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/24)]. Ibuprofen alone provided similar analgesia as the combined analgesia strategies and was associated with fewer adverse effects compared with ibuprofen plus hydromorphone. These findings confirm that nonopioid medications alone are sufficient for most children with acute musculoskeletal pain, and the addition of an opioid only increases the risk of adverse events. (See ["Pain in children: Approach to pain assessment and overview of management principles", section on 'Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pain-in-children-approach-to-pain-assessment-and-overview-of-management-principles?sectionName=Nonsteroidal+anti-inflammatory+drugs&topicRef=8365&anchor=H15&source=see_link#H15).)

Lumbar puncture in low-risk febrile neonates (December 2025)

Current guidelines advise lumbar puncture (LP) to evaluate for meningitis in all febrile neonates seen in the outpatient setting, with an option to omit LP in selected patients 22 to 28 days old at low risk. In a new meta-analysis of four prospective cohort studies (1537 previously healthy febrile, full-term neonates <28 days old [meningitis prevalence 0.7 percent]), of the 632 patients identified as low risk for invasive bacterial infection by the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) rule, none had meningitis (negative predictive value 99.96 percent) [[25](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/25)]. These findings suggest that it may be reasonable to omit LP in selected febrile neonates after shared decision-making with parents/primary caregivers as long as they are managed by experienced physicians and other clinicians in facilities with adequate resources to closely and safely monitor neonates. However, LP is still necessary in the majority of febrile neonates ≥7 days old. (See ["The febrile neonate (28 days of age or younger): Outpatient evaluation", section on '7 to 21 days old'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/the-febrile-neonate-28-days-of-age-or-younger-outpatient-evaluation?sectionName=7+to+21+days+old&topicRef=8365&anchor=H857933794&source=see_link#H857933794).)

Botulism associated with contaminated or unlicensed products (December 2025)

Although botulism is uncommon in the United States, recent cases have highlighted the risk of contaminated or unlicensed products. Between August and November 2025, 37 cases of infant botulism were linked to a particular brand of powdered formula (ByHeart) [[26](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/26)]; the causative organism, _Clostridium botulinum,_ was detected in several formula samples and all products from this brand were recalled. In addition, three unrelated cases of iatrogenic botulism were reported following self-injection of unlicensed botulinum toxin products purchased from various online vendors in Asia [[27](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/27)]. Clinicians should consider the possibility of botulism and evaluate for potential exposures in infants with acute onset of weak suck, ptosis, hypotonia, and/or constipation and in older individuals with features of acute cranial neuropathy (eg, ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia) and limb weakness, particularly if fever is absent. (See ["Botulism", section on 'Forms of botulism and their sources'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/botulism?sectionName=FORMS+OF+BOTULISM+AND+THEIR+SOURCES&topicRef=8365&anchor=H6&source=see_link#H6) and ["Neuromuscular junction disorders in newborns and infants", section on 'Infant botulism'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/neuromuscular-junction-disorders-in-newborns-and-infants?sectionName=INFANT+BOTULISM&topicRef=8365&anchor=H14&source=see_link#H14).)

PEDIATRIC RESUSCITATION

International guidelines for the management of pediatric sepsis and septic shock (May 2026)

The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Pediatric Guidelines for the management of sepsis and septic shock in children are available [[28](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/28)]. The guidelines reaffirm the prime importance of the rapid recognition of septic shock and treatment that includes timely administration of fluid bolus therapy, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, and, in patients not responding to fluid bolus therapy, initiation of vasoactive medications (epinephrine or norepinephrine) ([algorithm 1](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)). The 2026 guidelines also provide new recommendations that promote the use of blood lactate trends, lung and cardiac point-of-care ultrasound, and central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO 2 ≥ 70 percent) to monitor resuscitation. Our approach is consistent with these guidelines. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Approach'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Approach&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2493912177&source=see_link#H2493912177).)

Balanced crystalloid solution versus normal saline for children with septic shock (April 2026)

For children with septic shock, whether to administer balanced crystalloid solutions (BCS; for example, [lactated Ringer](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/lactated-ringer-solution-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)'s) versus normal [saline](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sodium-chloride-preparations-saline-and-oral-salt-tablets-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (NS) during initial fluid resuscitation is unclear. In a new randomized trial of over 8400 children with suspected septic shock, the combined outcomes of death, initiation of renal-replacement therapy, and persistent kidney dysfunction at 30 days were not significantly different in patients who were assigned to fluid resuscitation for up to 48 hours with BCS (3.4 percent) versus NS (3 percent) [[29](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/29)]. Hyperchloremia and hypernatremia were more common in patients receiving NS; increased blood lactate was more common in patients receiving BCS. Otherwise, adverse effects were similar in both groups. These findings suggest that either BCS or NS is an appropriate choice for fluid resuscitation of children with septic shock. However, the results may not be generalizable to patients with hospital-acquired sepsis or those treated in resource-limited settings. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Fluid resuscitation'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Fluid+resuscitation&topicRef=8365&anchor=H19450206&source=see_link#H19450206).)

2025 neonatal resuscitation guidelines (January 2026)

The American Heart Association/American Academy of Pediatrics/International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation/European Resuscitation Council (AHA/AAP/ILCOR/ERC) have published updated guidelines for neonatal resuscitation [[30-32](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/30-32)]. The guidelines reaffirm the previously published guidelines and neonatal resuscitative algorithm ([algorithm 2](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)). Modifications include updated recommendations for oxygen concentrations during initial resuscitation of preterm neonates (21 to 30 percent if 32 to <35 weeks of gestation, ≥30 percent if <32 weeks of gestation to achieve target oxygen saturation goals); initial peak inflation pressures (20 to 25 cm H 2 O if <32 weeks of gestation, 25 to 30 cm H 2 O if ≥32 weeks of gestation); measurement of endotracheal tube (ETT) insertion depth from tip to upper gum instead of tip to lip; and smaller ETT sizes for premature/low birth weight neonates. (See ["Neonatal resuscitation in the delivery room", section on 'Overview of approach'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/neonatal-resuscitation-in-the-delivery-room?sectionName=Overview+of+approach&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2429918249&source=see_link#H2429918249).)

2025 pediatric advanced life support and basic life support guidelines (December 2025)

The American Heart Association (AHA) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) have published updated guidelines for Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) and Basic Life Support (BLS). The PALS guidelines reaffirm the emergency management of children with [bradycardia](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FAlgorithm-PALS-Bradycardia-250121.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=q1pyrfBCbwFQJhc%2FMhbXjoDdj37GKNcvBArRruz4pi6prBWUwv9beMvsqP%2FK2xAfbvK884G79KE6fdnFMRXMM4fZAcZ5TzU5KFZrr6%2B23CknCjswgsstcbNI3gFKwwenEkwPM2igGHKUxJXjffIQ8On7WMAqa%2BQE8j%2BSsDFvZM4%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365), [tachycardia](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FAlgorithm-PALS-Tachyarrhythmia-250117.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=bMVDu3EwdQxRH00JMQHDLRQwGh1cclKlOyJ0Sl09whnFFbUzXKhrVbaEd0twQsKDKZjLqxYL5bwFayuhT%2FmkzZ0d%2FE6OdY%2F3%2BgP5rQmOblEgtT9hTOIra%2F%2Bln2i5svyPWGqh95oZeYA7moAvA%2FOIk%2BltqJ183iDuQJnlXkoVZgg%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365), and [pulseless arrest](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FAlgorithm-PALS-CA-250123.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=1lOXrl%2BAUwYFmmQHMw%2BxoR268snn0ENhenLHVT3D6c4bcZBFrNH%2F1HzPV2NrM9tbTMnz%2F0fSV%2B5hrAopPfQH6oKx9IyimzNo6fX%2BOAopVjZKTuKmCoo8d7Kpsf91LV9EHBS7jb49W6DIr7zXUYKCNA%3D%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365). During cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), PALS advises end-tidal CO 2 monitoring when feasible and new diastolic blood pressure goals of 25 mmHg in infants and ≥30 mmHg in children when invasive arterial monitoring is available [[33](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/33)]. Important changes to the pediatric BLS [guidance](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FFigure-10-Pediatric-BLS-Algorithm-2-or-more-Rescuers.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=b0aL%2FnN446ptMOOUoUchsjAVkGAnJoJSFCzpYBbuTOw7bTBt%2F7EnUJBbs8aoceEvBMuSYIFfIOZL%2BqZZA6yLwPasi9oeyYlUfTQ3nOV5z7FlWi1YmCy5L5yFJYzKjlfzA%2BR92e7gaavzgGcH9HppR%2FGPazKDGT3FWu5cmydfre4%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365)include new recommendations for the heel-of-one-hand or the thumb-encircling technique when performing cardiac compressions in infants (the two-finger technique is **not**recommended) and administration of [naloxone](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/naloxone-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) during CPR when an opioid overdose is suspected [[34](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/34)]. We agree with these guidelines. PRIMARY CARE ORTHOPEDICS AND SPORTS MEDICINE

Management of severely displaced distal radius fractures in children (April 2026)

For children with severely displaced distal radius fractures, the usual approach is fracture reduction and casting by a clinician or orthopedic surgeon with pediatric expertise. In a pragmatic trial of 750 children (4 to 10 years old) with severely displaced distal radial fractures, patients with markedly displaced Salter-Harris I or II physeal or metaphyseal fractures, were randomized to surgical reduction and casting versus casting alone [[35](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/35)]. At three months, functional outcomes, pain, and quality of life measured by validated scores as well as subjective cosmesis were significantly better in the surgical group. However, the difference in scores was small and less than minimally important differences for each outcome and became nonsignificant along with cosmesis at 12 months. These findings suggest that casting alone by an experienced clinician or orthopedic surgeon may be a reasonable option in children <10 years old with these injuries. However, we continue to support prompt reduction and casting pending further confirmation of these results. (See ["Distal forearm fractures in children: Initial management", section on 'Complete fracture'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/distal-forearm-fractures-in-children-initial-management?sectionName=Complete+fracture&topicRef=8365&anchor=H34&source=see_link#H34) and ["Distal forearm fractures in children: Initial management", section on 'Displaced Salter-Harris I or II fractures'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/distal-forearm-fractures-in-children-initial-management?sectionName=Displaced+Salter-Harris+I+or+II+fractures&topicRef=8365&anchor=H26&source=see_link#H26).)

Persistent symptoms of concussion in young children (March 2026)

In a prospective study, 235 young children (median age 2.4 years, 98 percent with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 15) were diagnosed with concussion in the emergency department (ED) based on the GCS score and ≥1 of the following: palpable skull fracture, headache (in verbal patients), altered mental status, or loss of consciousness [[36](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/36)]. At one month, 28 percent had persistent symptoms on a parent-reported symptoms score. This rate was significantly higher than in controls with orthopedic injuries undergoing ED evaluation and community children. On adjusted analysis, ED symptom severity was the primary predictor of persistent symptoms. These findings suggest that, similar to older children and adolescents, young children appear to have a significant risk of persistent symptoms of concussion after a mild head injury that appears to be associated with the severity of symptoms at initial evaluation. (See ["Concussion in children and adolescents: Management", section on 'Prognosis'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/concussion-in-children-and-adolescents-management?sectionName=PROGNOSIS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2832537&source=see_link#H2832537).)

Management of displaced medial epicondyle elbow fractures in children (January 2026)

For children with medial epicondyle elbow fractures, the degree of displacement that warrants operative intervention is debated. A multicenter pragmatic trial of 334 children with these fractures (24 percent with associated reducible elbow dislocations) randomly assigned patients to immobilization (typically cast or splinting) versus surgical treatment [[37](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/37)]. At 12 months after injury, functional outcomes, participation in sports and performing arts, pain, and quality of life were similar in the two groups; children assigned to surgery had more complications. These findings suggest that nonsurgical treatment is appropriate for most children with closed, displaced medial epicondyle elbow fractures. Surgical repair is still necessary for selected fractures complicated by an entrapped bony fragment in the elbow joint, ulnar nerve dysfunction, irreducible dislocation, or elbow instability. (See ["Epicondylar and transphyseal elbow fractures in children", section on 'Medial epicondylar fractures'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/epicondylar-and-transphyseal-elbow-fractures-in-children?sectionName=Medial+epicondylar+fractures&topicRef=8365&anchor=H17&source=see_link#H17).)

TOXICOLOGY

Poisoning-related fatality from illicit substances in children and adolescents (May 2026)

Illicit substances such as opioids can result in poisoning-related fatality in pediatric patients. In an analysis conducted on national surveillance databases from the Centers for Disease Control, the rate of death from poisoning (including illicit drug overdoses) in children and adolescents aged 1 to 19 years increased by 12.7 percent from 2020 to 2023 [[38](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/38)]. In 2023, 1913 deaths were from illicit drug overdoses, and the majority (79.5 percent) were from [fentanyl](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link). These findings confirm that illicit substances remain a common cause of fatality in children and adolescents, and that ongoing educational and other preventive measures are warranted in this population. (See ["Poisoning in children: Prevention", section on 'Fatalities'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/poisoning-in-children-prevention?sectionName=Fatalities&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2&source=see_link#H2).)

Poisoning-related injury from ingested household products in young children (May 2026)

Ingested household products remain a common cause of poisoning-related injury in young children. An analysis of national surveillance data estimated that over 240,000 children aged ≤5 years were treated in United States emergency departments for injuries from exposure to household cleaning products from 2007 to 2022 [[39](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/39)]. Approximately 60 percent of injuries were from ingestion. The products and containers associated with the most injuries were bleach (30.1 percent), detergents (28.6 percent), detergent packets (33 percent), and spray bottles (28.2 percent). These findings highlight the importance of ongoing educational, regulatory, and product engineering measures to prevent injuries from ingested substances in pediatric patients. (See ["Poisoning in children: Prevention", section on 'Ingested substances'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/poisoning-in-children-prevention?sectionName=Ingested+substances&topicRef=8365&anchor=H108484245&source=see_link#H108484245).)

Rome V diagnostic criteria for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (April 2026)

Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) is a clinical diagnosis. The Rome V criteria, which update the commonly used Rome IV criteria, were recently published [[40](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/40)]. A patient meets the Rome V criteria for CHS if all of the following are present:

●Stereotypical episodic vomiting resembling cyclic vomiting syndrome in terms of onset, duration, and frequency

●Presentation after prolonged (one year) and excessive cannabis use (≥4 days per week or ≥15 doses per week, or both)

●Relief of vomiting episodes by sustained cessation of cannabis use (at least six months or three typical emetic cycles)

Association with pathologic bathing behavior (prolonged hot baths or showers) is supportive but not necessary. We agree that these criteria can assist in diagnosing CHS. (See ["Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome", section on 'Diagnostic criteria'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/cannabinoid-hyperemesis-syndrome?sectionName=Diagnostic+criteria&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3072534301&source=see_link#H3072534301).)

New recommendations on use of activated charcoal for overdoses (April 2026)

[Activated charcoal](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/activated-charcoal-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (AC) adsorbs chemicals within minutes of contact, preventing gastrointestinal (GI) absorption and subsequent toxicity. Indications and timing are debatable, and "routine" use for GI decontamination has not demonstrated reduced morbidity and mortality in poisoned patients. Newly released recommendations from the Clinical Toxicology Recommendations Collaborative (which included representatives from three toxicology societies) suggest a potential benefit for a slightly prolonged window for AC administration for ingestion of certain agents (eg, [acetaminophen](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acetaminophen-paracetamol-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), salicylates, and [verapamil](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/verapamil-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) and an additional dose of AC for agents with potential for prolonged GI tract persistence (aforementioned agents as well as [carbamazepine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/carbamazepine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), [valproic acid](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/valproate-valproic-acid-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), paraquat, [phenobarbital](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/phenobarbital-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), and [theophylline](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/theophylline-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) [[41](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/41)]. We agree with most of the recommendations from the Collaborative. (See ["Gastrointestinal decontamination of the poisoned patient", section on 'Indications'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/gastrointestinal-decontamination-of-the-poisoned-patient?sectionName=Indications&topicRef=8365&anchor=H18993776&source=see_link#H18993776).)

Trends in kratom exposures reported to United States poison centers (March 2026)

Kratom (_Mitragyna speciosa_) is a natural product derived from a tree native to Southeast Asia used for its stimulant, analgesic, and antidepressant properties. Commercially sold kratom products can have alkaloidal concentrations that are different compared with natural leaf products, which can cause toxicity and dependence. There were over 14,000 kratom exposures reported to United States poison centers between 2015 and 2025 [[42](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/42)]. Reports steadily increased through 2019, plateaued through 2024, and surged in 2025 (over 3400 reported exposures). Reports involving multiple substances (eg, opioids) were more likely to cause serious outcomes and hospitalization. These findings suggest that kratom-related adverse effects are increasing in the United States. (See ["Kratom health effects from acute and chronic use", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/kratom-health-effects-from-acute-and-chronic-use?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2211216297&source=see_link#H2211216297).)

Chronic lead exposure and increased cardiovascular mortality (March 2026)

Cumulative lead exposure has been linked to an increased risk of atherosclerosis, cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality, and all-cause mortality. A study of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 1999 to 2014, including over 42,000 individuals, reported that higher estimated bone lead levels were associated with increased CVD mortality; the group with the greatest lead burden had an 88 percent increase in adjusted mortality risk compared with estimated preindustrial levels [[43](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/43)]. This corresponds to an estimated 3.5 million deaths globally in 2023 attributable to elevated bone lead levels, which would account for almost 6 percent of deaths and would make lead exposure the eighth leading risk for global mortality. These findings highlight the need to screen for and mitigate occupational and environmental lead exposure. (See ["Lead exposure, toxicity, and poisoning in adults: Clinical manifestations and diagnosis", section on 'Chronic and long-term exposure effects'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/lead-exposure-toxicity-and-poisoning-in-adults-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Chronic+and+long-term+exposure+effects&topicRef=8365&anchor=H7&source=see_link#H7).)

Causes and prognosis of acquired methemoglobinemia (March 2026)

Acquired methemoglobinemia is a potentially life-threatening condition in which the iron in heme becomes oxidized and cannot deliver oxygen. In a new study from Thailand that evaluated 169 individuals with acquired methemoglobinemia over a 10-year period, the most common causes were [dapsone](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/dapsone-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (in 30 percent) and the contact herbicide propanil (in 27 percent, mostly for self-harm) [[44](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/44)]. Approximately 10 percent had glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. The fatality rate was 11 percent, 40 percent were admitted to the intensive care unit, 34 percent required intubation, and 89 percent were hospitalized. These data reinforce the importance of rapid recognition and treatment of this condition. (See ["Methemoglobinemia", section on 'Most common acquired causes'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/methemoglobinemia?sectionName=Most+common+acquired+causes&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3113698015&source=see_link#H3113698015).)

Cardiotoxicity of supratherapeutic loperamide exposures (March 2026)

The antidiarrheal agent [loperamide](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/loperamide-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) has been reported to cause ventricular conduction disturbances, including QRS and QT interval prolongation, idioventricular rhythm, and ventricular tachycardia, following overdose. Loperamide is a synthetic opioid but does not typically cause classic signs of opioid toxicity. A systematic review of almost 130 cases of supratherapeutic loperamide exposure found that severe toxicity has been reported at daily doses as low as 20 to 40 mg [[45](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/45)]. Syncope was reported in almost half of cases, while severe cases mainly had polymorphic or sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. These findings suggest that patients with supratherapeutic loperamide exposure may benefit from cardiac monitoring. (See ["Acute opioid intoxication in adults", section on 'Loperamide'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-opioid-intoxication-in-adults?sectionName=Loperamide&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2282453505&source=see_link#H2282453505).)

Psilocybin use in Oregon and Colorado following decriminalization (March 2026)

Psilocybin is a hallucinogen found in many species of mushrooms and has been studied for the treatment of various mental health disorders. Psilocybin was decriminalized for use in licensed clinics in Oregon in 2020 and Colorado in 2022. A study of data from a national survey of drug use from 2018 to 2025 found that self-reported use increased in both states following decriminalization (mean prevalence increased from 2 to 4.5 percent and 2.7 to 4.3 percent in Oregon and Colorado, respectively) [[46](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/46)]. This increase was greater than a weighted composite control of the other states. These findings may impact policy decisions regarding psilocybin decriminalization for therapeutic use. (See ["Intoxication from LSD and other common hallucinogens", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/intoxication-from-lsd-and-other-common-hallucinogens?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H57999532&source=see_link#H57999532).)

Test characteristics of an enzymatic ethylene glycol assay (March 2026)

Ethylene glycol poisoning is potentially fatal if not treated promptly. Diagnosis can be challenging since ethylene glycol concentrations are usually performed by gas chromatography, which is not widely available and typically has long turn-around times. A modification to a glycerol dehydrogenase-based assay approved for veterinary use has been externally validated and is used by some hospitals; it can be performed 24/7 and has a typical turn-around time of several hours. A study of over 400 samples analyzed by both an enzymatic assay and chromatography found a sensitivity and specificity of 89 and 83 percent, respectively [[47](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/47)]. All four false-negative enzymatic results were below the 20 mg/dL treatment threshold. These results suggest that an enzymatic ethylene glycol assay may be a valuable screening tool. (See ["Methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning: Pharmacology, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis", section on 'Testing for methanol and ethylene glycol'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/methanol-and-ethylene-glycol-poisoning-pharmacology-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Testing+for+methanol+and+ethylene+glycol&topicRef=8365&anchor=H12&source=see_link#H12).)

ED-initiated injectable extended-release buprenorphine (February 2026)

Previous studies have found that emergency department (ED) initiation of sublingual [buprenorphine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/buprenorphine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is associated with decreased all-cause and opioid-related mortality and is feasible and cost-effective. A new trial with almost 2000 ED patients who had untreated opioid use disorder and signs of withdrawal found that ED patients started on extended-release injectable buprenorphine, compared with sublingual buprenorphine, had similar engagement in opioid use disorder treatment at 7 (41 versus 39 percent) and 30 days (44 versus 45 percent) [[48](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/48)]. The rate of precipitated withdrawal was similar and rare (<1 percent) in both groups despite a high prevalence of [fentanyl](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) dependence (76 percent). These results suggest that initiation of extended-release injectable buprenorphine may be a safe and feasible option in ED patients for treatment of an opioid use disorder. (See ["Acute opioid intoxication in adults", section on 'Prevention of recurrent opioid overdose'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-opioid-intoxication-in-adults?sectionName=PREVENTION+OF+RECURRENT+OPIOID+OVERDOSE&topicRef=8365&anchor=H10057659&source=see_link#H10057659).)

Impact of arsenic exposure reduction on chronic disease mortality (December 2025)

Chronic exposure to inorganic arsenic has been associated with increased all-cause, cancer, and cardiovascular mortality. Prior studies found population-level improvements in mortality following arsenic mitigation efforts, but individual-level evidence is lacking. An 18-year study that followed almost 11,000 patients in Bangladesh exposed to arsenic in drinking water found a dose-response association between reduced arsenic exposure and lower mortality [[49](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/49)]. Each decrease in the interquartile range of urine arsenic concentration (approximately 200 mcg/g creatinine) was associated with a 22, 20, and 23 percent decrease in chronic disease, cancer, and cardiovascular disease mortality, respectively. These findings support the essential steps in managing chronic arsenic poisoning: identifying the source, mitigating the exposure, and eliminating ongoing and future exposure. (See ["Arsenic exposure and chronic poisoning", section on 'Preventing ongoing exposure'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/arsenic-exposure-and-chronic-poisoning?sectionName=Preventing+ongoing+exposure&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1562828577&source=see_link#H1562828577).)

Increased United States Emergency Department visits for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (December 2025)

Previous studies have reported rising rates of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS), which causes episodic vomiting and intense abdominal pain in some individuals with prolonged, nearly daily cannabis use. A cross-sectional study of over 188 million United States emergency department (ED) visits found that from 2016 to 2020, visits for CHS sharply increased from 4 to 33 per 100,000 visits, and have since plateaued but remain elevated [[50](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/50)]. These findings highlight the medical burden of CHS, can help inform policy, and should remind ED clinicians to ask about cannabis use in patients with cyclic vomiting and abdominal pain. (See ["Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/cannabinoid-hyperemesis-syndrome?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2281824146&source=see_link#H2281824146).)

TRAUMA

PECARN cervical spine injury prediction rule performance by patient age (May 2026)

In a planned subanalysis of the cohort of 22,430 children used to develop the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Cervical Spine Injury (CSI) prediction rule ([algorithm 3](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)), age-specific rules were derived based on developmental transition (0 to <2 years, 2 to <8 years, 8 to <16 years, and 16 to <18 years) [[51](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/51)]. When compared with the PECARN CSI rule, testing characteristics were similar for the age-specific rules; the negative predictive value for the PECARN CSI rule (99.9 percent, prevalence of CSI 1.9 percent) equaled or exceeded all age-specific rules. These findings support the use of the PECARN CSI rule to determine the risk of CSI and the need for C-spine imaging in infants and children of all ages. (See ["Evaluation and acute management of cervical spine injuries in children and adolescents", section on 'Indications and choice of imaging'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-acute-management-of-cervical-spine-injuries-in-children-and-adolescents?sectionName=Indications+and+choice+of+imaging&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2844494741&source=see_link#H2844494741).)

Prehospital whole blood transfusion for traumatic hemorrhage (March 2026)

Two recent trials have examined the efficacy and safety of prehospital transfusion of low-titer, group O whole blood (LTOWB) versus blood components by Emergency Medical Services (EMS):

●In a pragmatic trial of over 600 patients with life-threatening bleeding transported by air ambulances in England, patients were transfused up to 2 units of LTOWB versus red cells plus plasma [[52](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/52)]. The composite of mortality plus massive transfusion within 24 hours and 90-day call-cause mortality was similar between the groups; the LTOWB group had slightly fewer serious adverse events.

●In another pragmatic trial of over 1000 patients with trauma and hypotension transported by air bases in the United States, either from the scene or from a referring emergency department, patients were transfused up to 2 units of LTOWB versus red cells, plasma, or both. Mortality at 30 days was similar (26 versus 21 percent) between LTOWB and components, as was in-hospital mortality, blood product requirements, and adverse events [[53](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/53)].

These findings suggest that use of LTOWB, which is logistically simpler than components, is a reasonable option for EMS with prehospital transfusion programs. (See ["Initial management of moderate to severe hemorrhage in the adult trauma patient", section on 'Transfusion'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/initial-management-of-moderate-to-severe-hemorrhage-in-the-adult-trauma-patient?sectionName=Transfusion&topicRef=8365&anchor=H749310297&source=see_link#H749310297).)

Comparison of C-spine injury prediction rules in children (January 2026)

The Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) C-spine injury rule ([algorithm 3](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)) demonstrates high accuracy for identifying C-spine injury in pediatric blunt trauma patients while lowering the use of computed tomography (CT) imaging, but evidence comparing it to other prediction rules commonly used in adult trauma centers is limited. A secondary analysis of the PECARN rule cohort (22,430 children) compared it with the National Emergency X-Radiography Utilization Study Low Risk (NEXUS) criteria and the Canadian Cervical Spine (C-spine) Rule (CCR) [[54](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/54)]. The results showed that the PECARN rule had higher sensitivity and negative predictive value for C-spine injury than the other two rules, with a lower projected CT imaging rate (PECARN 6.9 percent, NEXUS 10.8 percent, and CCR 13.2 percent). These findings support the use of the PECARN C-spine injury rule in children with blunt trauma rather than guidelines primarily or solely derived from adult patients. (See ["Evaluation and acute management of cervical spine injuries in children and adolescents", section on 'Indications and choice of imaging'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-acute-management-of-cervical-spine-injuries-in-children-and-adolescents?sectionName=Indications+and+choice+of+imaging&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2844494741&source=see_link#H2844494741).)

Timing of tranexamic acid after trauma (December 2025)

Previous studies have found that [tranexamic acid](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/tranexamic-acid-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (TXA), an antifibrinolytic agent, reduces mortality if given within three hours of injury in patients with significant hemorrhage, but the greatest benefit may occur when TXA is given sooner. In a secondary analysis of the Prehospital Tranexamic Acid for Severe Trauma (PATCH-Trauma) trial, the 28-day mortality benefit was only present if TXA was administered within 90 minutes (17 percent TXA versus 25 percent placebo), while there was no benefit if administered between 90 and 180 minutes (18 percent TXA versus 17 percent placebo) [[55](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/55)]. These findings suggest that the benefit of TXA is greatest if given early after injury. (See ["Initial management of moderate to severe hemorrhage in the adult trauma patient", section on 'Patient within three hours of injury'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/initial-management-of-moderate-to-severe-hemorrhage-in-the-adult-trauma-patient?sectionName=Patient+within+three+hours+of+injury&topicRef=8365&anchor=H30549926&source=see_link#H30549926).)

results.title: Prevalence of long-term right ventricular dysfunction after acute pulmonary embolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis
results.content:
Recently, Alizadehasl et,al2700330-9/fulltext#bib27) demonstrated that patients with a higher RV/LV ratio, lower TASPE and lower right ventricular free wall strain at discharge were more likely to develop PPEI at 6-months, indicating the relationship between long-term condition of the right ventricle and symptoms of functional impairment. Also, apart from the high incidence, incomplete recovery of the right ventricle had also a high adjusted OR (12.5, 95% CI 3.33–45.45) for predicting an intermediate-to-high probability of pulmonary hypertension. The PEITHO trial reported that the incomplete recovery of echocardiographic parameters at 6-months strongly predicted PPEI or CTEPH.1900330-9/fulltext#bib19) PPES is defined as new or progressive dyspnea, exercise intolerance and/or impaired [...] _Eur Heart J._ 2019; 40(11):902-910

[...] Long-term sequela of acute PE, such as chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease (CTEPD), RVD, post-PE impairment (PPEI) and PPES, etc. have been increasingly emphasised in recent years.2100330-9/fulltext#bib21) Prospective studies reported CTEPH incidence of 2.3%–5.25% and CTEPD of 5.75% at 2-years after acute PE.22–2500330-9/fulltext#bib22) Remarkably, RVD was much higher in prevalence than CTEPH after acute PE, which has been inferred that residual clot due to incomplete thrombus resolution lead to a poor recovery of right ventricular function,2600330-9/fulltext#bib26) while incomplete thrombus resolution occurs in 25–50% of patients after acute PE despite adequate anticoagulation.900330-9/fulltext#bib9)

## Summary

### Background

Right ventricular dysfunction (RVD) is associated with adverse outcomes of acute pulmonary embolism (PE). However, there are no studies describing the long-term, full-spectrum right ventricular parameters on morphology, pressure and function at certain follow-up time points after PE onset. More exploration of right ventricular function would provide useful clues for long-term management of patients with PE.

### Methods

For this systematic review and meta-analysis, we completed a literature search in Pubmed, EMBASE and WebofScience (from Jan 1st, 1998 to April 20th, 2023). Studies of patients with acute PE followed-up longer than 3 months with right ventricle assessment and written in English-language were included. Right ventricular function was assessed by either echocardiography or computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA). The primary outcome was structural and functional parameters of the right ventricle, and the secondary outcomes were functional assessments [New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification and 6-min walk test distance (6 MWD)], at each follow-up time points. Random effect meta-analyses were performed using R software (PROSPERO: CRD42023433332).

### Findings

A total of 33 studies (3920 patients) were included in the final analysis. The 3-month, 6-month and 1-year prevalence of right ventricular dysfunction (RVD) was 0.34 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.21–0.48, I 2=96%], 0.26 (95% CI 0.17–0.36, I 2=93%) and 0.34 (95% CI 0.19–0.48, I 2=94%), respectively. Pooled tricuspid annulus plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), right ventricular to left ventricular diameter (RV/LV) ratio and pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) at 1-year was 21.80 mm (95% CI 20.08–23.52, I 2=93%), 0.64 (95% CI 0.48–0.81, I 2=92%) and 27.33 mmHg (95% CI 18.88–35.78) (I 2=96%), respectively. The proportion of NYHA III–IV was 0.06 (95% CI 0.0–0.12) and the pooled 6 MWD was 462.98 m (95% CI 447.55–478.41) over 1 year. Patients treated with thrombolysis had lower prevalence of RVD (1-year 0.17 and 0.07 in systemic thrombolysis and catheter-directed thrombolysis, respectively) than those treated with anticoagulation therapy alone (1-year 0.24) but the pooled risk ratio (RR) was not statistically significant.

### Interpretation

Although the conclusion of this study may be limited by its high heterogeneity from varied study designs, inclusion criteria and definition of RVD of each study, our findings suggested that persistent RVD and functional impairment were of considerable high prevalence during long-term follow-up after acute PE. Treatment strategy may influence the prevalence of long-term RVD.
